bib.title: OpenCodeInterpreter: Integrating Code Generation with Execution and Refinement

legacy_report:
SOURCE: OpenCodeInterpreter: Integrating Code Generation with Execution and Refinement. Tianyu Zheng, Ge Zhang, Tianhao Shen, Xueling Liu, Bill Yuchen Lin, Jie Fu, Wenhu Chen, Xiang Yue. arXiv:2402.14658v3 (cs.SE), 7 Jan 2025. The venue is not printed in the text; I treat it as a preprint. The EvalPlus leaderboard snapshot used is dated 10 Feb 2024.

COVERAGE: All 99,947 chars were extracted. I read the main text, tables 1-5, limitations, references (skimmed) and appendices A-D (prompts). Appendix E (example dialogues) was skimmed only. Figures A1/A2 (data-filtering counts, language pie) are images, so their numbers are not extractable. The target note was read as well. It does not cite this paper, and the paper has no Reflexion, DGM or evolve-loop content.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Execution feedback (up to 2 rounds) lifts the 33B model to roughly GPT-4 Turbo single-turn level. Synthetic human feedback lifts it further.
  number: 83.2 (76.4) avg with execution feedback, versus 79.0 (70.4) single-turn. GPT-4 Turbo single-turn is 84.2 (76.2). Synthetic human feedback gives 88.0 (81.0), and the oracle variant gives 91.6 (84.6).
  setup: OpenCodeInterpreter-DS-33B, average over HumanEval and MBPP (EvalPlus "plus" scores in brackets), pass@1, greedy decoding, max 2 refinement rounds. The human feedback is GPT-4-simulated.
  quote: "OpenCodeInterpreter-33B achieves an accuracy of 83.2 (76.4) on the average (and plus versions) of HumanEval and MBPP, closely rivaling GPT-4's 84.2 (76.2) and further elevates to 91.6 (84.6) with synthesized human feedback from GPT-4."
  where: Abstract; Table 1 (~chars 14,000-21,000, 33B block).
- Claim: The "oracle" feedback gain is partly leakage. The oracle GPT-4 sees the ground-truth canonical solution, so 91.6 is an upper bound, not a deployable result.
  number: 91.6 (84.6) oracle vs 88.0 (81.0) non-oracle (33B)
  setup: Same as above. The prompt says to guide without revealing the canonical solution.
  quote: "GPT-4 also accesses the ground-truth solution, offering insight into OpenCodeInterpreter's optimal performance in code refinement when guided by precise feedback."
  where: Section 3 Evaluation Setup; Appendix D.
- Claim: Execution feedback helps the baselines too, but unevenly. GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-3.5 gain on average. WizardCoder-33B and Magicoder-S-DS-6.7B get worse with execution feedback. This means refinement is not free. A loop can degrade a model that was not trained to use the feedback.
  number: GPT-4 Turbo 84.2 (76.2) -> 90.0 (81.2). GPT-3.5 Turbo 77.2 (67.7) -> 81.9 (72.3). WizardCoder-V1.1 33B 79.4 (70.1) -> 77.2 (68.9). Magicoder-S-DS 6.7B 76.3 (67.6) -> 75.3 (67.2).
  setup: Table 1, averages, max 2 rounds. Baseline numbers are copied from the EvalPlus leaderboard or replicated from official checkpoints.
  quote: "WizardCoder-V1.1 (Luo et al., 2023) 79.9 (73.2) 78.9 (66.9) 79.4 (70.1) + Execution Feedback 33B Instruct • ◦ 74.4 (69.5) 79.9 (68.2) 77.2 (68.9)"
  where: Table 1 (~chars 17,000-20,000).
- Claim: The feedback gain holds at every scale tested, and it is larger for the weaker-single-turn models.
  number: 6.7B DS 75.1 (67.9) -> 81.9 (75.6); 13B CL 74.1 (66.5) -> 79.7 (72.0); 34B CL 75.7 (67.0) -> 81.0 (73.3); 70B CL 74.6 (66.3) -> 80.7 (73.7)
  setup: Table 1 averages, base models CodeLlama and DeepSeekCoder, 2 rounds.
  quote: "OpenCodeInterpreter-CL 76.2 (70.7) 73.0 (61.9) 74.6 (66.3) + Execution Feedback 70B Instruct • • 79.9 (77.4) 81.5 (69.9) 80.7 (73.7)"
  where: Table 1, 70B block.
- Claim: Training on multi-turn data is what makes the model benefit from feedback. The 0:1 mix (no single-turn data) vs 2:1 shows this, as does the Code-Feedback ablation (Table 3).
  number: Table 3: execution-feedback average rises from 77.5 (69.5) with Single-turn Packing alone to 79.1 (71.3) with packing + simulation + correction, and 81.9 (75.6) with the full set. Without execution feedback the full set scores 75.1 (67.9).
  setup: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B and 33B base. The 2:1 single-turn : Code-Feedback mix is best (Table 2).
  quote: "Code-Feedback (Full) ✔ 81.9 (75.6)"
  where: Table 3 (~chars 31,000-32,000).
- Claim: Mixing in high-quality single-turn data improves multi-turn performance. The best ratio is 2:1 (WizardCoder 110K : Code-Feedback).
  number: 2:1 with execution feedback gives 81.9 (75.6). 1:1 gives 78.2 (69.3). 0:1 gives 71.5 (74.0).
  setup: Table 2, soft-target fine-tuning, six ratios. The 0:1 MBPP cell "66.7 ( 76.6)" has the plus score above the base score, probably a typo in the paper.
  quote: "✗ 73.8 (68.9) 73.9 (62.9) 73.9 (65.9)0:1 ✔ 76.2 (71.3) 66.7 ( 76.6) 71.5 (74.0)"
  where: Table 2.
- Claim: The simulated data pipeline is a generate-execute-refine loop with a cap of three iterations. GPT-3.5 drafts, the code is executed, and GPT-4 gets the output and refines. It stops when GPT-4 thinks the answer is correct or after three rounds. The stop criterion is a model's own judgment.
  number: max 3 iterations; 51K examples from Interaction Simulation; 500 Code Correction; 16.6K from packing (105K single-turn sources)
  setup: Training data construction, 156K filtered queries (from 287K, complexity 4-5 by Qwen-72B-Chat, two prompts).
  quote: "This cycle is repeated until GPT-4 delivers what it deems a correct solution or until a maximum of three iterations is reached."
  where: Section 2.1.
- Claim: Code-Feedback is 68K dialogues and 192K turns, with ten feedback categories.
  number: 68K samples, 192K turns
  setup: Figure 2 table.
  quote: "Code-Feedback (Ours) 68K 192K ✔ ✔ ✔"
  where: Figure 2.
- Claim: Multi-turn improvement shows on MT-Bench coding questions (10 questions, GPT-4 scores 1-10). Second-turn gains over the same-base Instruct model are large.
  number: OpenCI-DS-33B second turn 6.7 (avg 6.8) vs DS-33B-Instruct 4.2 (avg 5.5). GPT-4 averages 8.6.
  setup: 10 coding questions, each with a follow-up.
  quote: "OpenCI-DS-33B 6.8 6.7 6.8 ... DS-33B-Instruct 6.7 4.2 5.5"
  where: Table 5.
- Claim: The leakage check is low-overlap but covers only line-level duplication.
  number: 5 consecutive lines: 1.19% HumanEval(+), 0.51% MBPP(+). 7 lines: 0.00% both.
  quote: "5 lines 1.19% 0.51%"
  where: Table 4.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "it may struggle with extremely complex or ambiguous user intents". Performance may vary by language and domain.
- Case study (Fig A10): the model fixed errors one at a time and exceeded the maximum of three attempts, so it fails with multiple simultaneous hard errors.
- The 2-round cap is imposed "to maintain fairness". More rounds are untested.
- "Human feedback" is GPT-4-simulated, not human. The human-feedback runs cover only 6.7B and 33B, "Due to budget constraints".
- The evaluation is HumanEval/MBPP, small function-level tasks with unit tests. There is no repository-level or long-horizon evaluation, no cost or latency figures, and no multi-seed variance. Greedy decoding, single run.
- This is a supervised fine-tuning method, not a runtime loop that edits itself. It trains the model to use feedback. It does not show a loop improving its own scaffold, harness or weights over iterations.
- Dated: baselines are from the Feb 2024 EvalPlus leaderboard (GPT-4 Turbo, CodeLlama, DeepSeekCoder). HumanEval/MBPP are likely saturated now.
- Training data is generated by GPT-3.5/GPT-4, so the gains are partly distillation from a stronger model and not self-improvement. The paper states that the initial training set had "significant presence of low-quality or incorrect data".

BUILDS ON: Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023). Self-debug (Chen et al., 2023, "Teaching large language models to self-debug"). EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023). HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021). MBPP (Austin et al., 2021). Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2023b). WizardCoder / Code Evol-Instruct (Luo et al., 2023). Magicoder (Wei et al., 2023). StepCoder (Dou et al., 2024), which uses RL with compiler feedback. CodeRL (Le et al., 2022). DebugBench (Tian et al., 2024). In-context pretraining (Shi et al., 2023), for the packing idea. MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2024). Base models CodeLlama (Roziere et al., 2023) and DeepSeek-Coder (Guo et al., 2024).

CODE: none worth keeping. The appendix has prompts only. One is a verbatim feedback-simulator rule that could fit the note's "structured verdict" theme: the JSON schema {"satisfied", "not_satisfied", "feedback"} with "Feedback must come from a point included in 'not_satisfied' field" (Appendix B).

FIGURES (not rendered; I did not run the captions script)
- Fig 1: pass@1 on HumanEval for 6.7B and 33B across Single Turn, w/ Exec Feedback, w/ Human Feedback and w/ H.F. (Oracle), against GPT-4 CI and GPT-3.5 CI. The extracted numbers are jumbled, so use Table 1 instead.
- Fig 2: dataset construction pipeline and comparison table. It explains the five data sources quickly.
- Fig A10: a failure case, in which the model fixed errors one at a time and hit the three-attempt cap.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction of Figure 1 and the Table 1 row labels is jumbled (the "+ Execution Feedback" rows are separated from their model names). I attributed rows by position and cross-checked with the abstract's 83.2/76.4/91.6/84.6.
- The Table 2 cell "66.7 ( 76.6)" looks like a typo.
- No embedded instructions found. The prompts in Appendices B-D are dataset-construction prompts, not directed at me.
- Relevance to note 08: the paper is weak support for the note's self-improving-loop claims. Its strongest transferable points are that execution feedback gives a measurable multi-turn gain, that some models regress with feedback, and that "oracle" feedback is an upper bound. It is a fine-tuning paper, not about a loop that rewrites itself, and it reports no cost figures.
